## Developing a research topic

- **Research question:** what you want to learn
- **Setting:** institutional context relevant to answering the question
- **Data:** empirical measurements relevant to answering the question

::: {.notes}
Introduce the three components before discussing either paper. Then work
through question, setting, and data for each paper in turn. This keeps the
definitions available for reference and gives each example a continuous
narrative.

Students may begin with a question, an interesting institution, or a dataset.
The eventual project needs all three to fit together.
:::

## Research question

- Specific enough to answer empirically
- Motivated by an economic theory or a substantive policy issue
- May concern a [causal]{.fg style="--col: #107895"} effect or a [descriptive]{.fg style="--col: #9a2515"} relationship

::: {.notes}
A topic such as housing or insurance is broader than a research question.
A question specifies what we want to learn: an effect, a comparison, or a
pattern.

A descriptive relationship can be a research contribution when it informs
an economic explanation. Students do not have to force every idea into a
causal design. They should be able to explain why the answer matters and
what it adds to existing work.
:::

## Setting

- Institutional details relevant to answering the question
- [Causal]{.fg style="--col: #107895"}: variation supporting a credible comparison to an unobserved counterfactual
- [Descriptive]{.fg style="--col: #9a2515"}: a context in which theory has testable predictions

::: {.notes}
For a causal question, the relevant institutional detail might be an
assignment rule or the timing of a policy or event. The setting includes
the source of identifying variation.

Define the counterfactual as what would have happened without the treatment.
It is unobserved for the treated group, so the design needs a comparison
that can credibly represent it.

For a descriptive question, understanding the choices people face helps
us interpret observed relationships. The distinction between setting and
data is their role: the setting explains why a comparison is informative;
the data allow us to make it.
:::

## Data

- Quantifiable measures relevant to answering the question
- May be numeric or constructed from text, images, and other records

::: {.notes}
Separate what needs to be measured from the name of a dataset. Check the
questionnaire or documentation for the actual variables, population,
dates, and identifiers.

Original work can use an established dataset in a new way or combine
existing sources to answer a new question. Neither route requires
collecting a new survey.

For example, text can be classified by topic or assigned a sentiment score.
The measurement still needs to capture the concept of interest; turning
text into a number does not by itself make that number informative.
:::

## Initial ideas

3 minutes, individually

- Write one economic theory or policy issue that interests you.
- Formulate a specific research question about it.
- Explain what we would learn from the answer.

::: {.notes}
Have students write in their notebooks. A tentative question is sufficient;
no setting or data source is required yet. The examples that follow show
how these other components can develop.

If useful, invite two students to share and discuss whether each question
specifies something that could be answered.
:::

## Two examples

[Descriptive: private information in insurance markets]{.fg style="--col: #9a2515"}\
[Finkelstein and McGarry (2006), American Economic Review (Finkelstein is an MIT professor)](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2022-08/Multiple%20Dimensions%20of%20Private%20Information-%20Eviden.pdf){style="color: inherit; font-weight: inherit;"}

[Causal: local effects of large, mixed-income housing]{.fg style="--col: #107895"}\
[Odayappan (2026), Journal of Housing Economics (Harvard undergraduate senior thesis)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1051137726000240){style="color: inherit; font-weight: inherit;"}

::: {.notes}
Introduce both papers before discussing either in detail. The insurance
paper revisits a classic theory of market failure. The housing paper
investigates a current policy concern. Both will be discussed in the same
order: research question, setting, data, and findings.

References: [Finkelstein and McGarry (2006)](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2022-08/Multiple%20Dimensions%20of%20Private%20Information-%20Eviden.pdf);
[Odayappan (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1051137726000240).
:::

## [Insurance]{.fg style="--col: #9a2515"}: research question

Do insurance buyers have private information relevant
to their risk?

- Adverse selection as a source of market failure: the “market for lemons”

::: {.notes}
The paper is “Multiple Dimensions of Private Information: Evidence from
the Long-Term Care Insurance Market.”

Recall the logic of the market for lemons: information that one party
has and the other lacks can affect who participates in a market. In this
application, buyers may know more about their likely need for care than
the insurer does. Define long-term care insurance as coverage for expenses
such as nursing-home care.

The motivation starts with a classic economic idea and asks how it works
in an actual market. Amy Finkelstein is an
[MIT economics professor](https://economics.mit.edu/people/faculty/amy-finkelstein).
:::

## [Insurance]{.fg style="--col: #9a2515"}: setting

- Supplemental insurance for long-term care expenses in the U.S.
- Insurers assess risk when offering coverage and setting premiums
- Individuals choose whether to buy coverage
- Positive correlation test between insurance choice and risk realization

::: {.notes}
Voluntary purchase is the institutional feature that allows selection:
people can choose coverage based on what they know about their own risk.
Insurers also assess applicants, so private information means information
beyond what insurers already know or use. Differences in age or known
health alone do not establish it.

Supplemental here refers to private coverage alongside public programs
and out-of-pocket payment for care. It is not Medigap insurance.

Source: [Finkelstein and McGarry (2006), sections I–II](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2022-08/Multiple%20Dimensions%20of%20Private%20Information-%20Eviden.pdf).
:::

## [Insurance]{.fg style="--col: #9a2515"}: data

Health and Retirement Study: a public survey of aging, health, and finances

- Long-term care insurance ownership and subsequent nursing-home use
- Respondents’ own beliefs about their future likelihood of needing care

::: {.notes}
The authors use the AHEAD cohort, observing insurance and expectations in
1995 and nursing-home use through 2000. The expectations question asks
respondents to assess their own chance of entering a nursing home within
five years. These questions make an established survey useful for testing
private information.

The paper also uses insurer application forms and an actuarial model to
approximate insurers' information. The public survey is the core source,
but learning how insurers assess risk is part of the research.

Sources: [paper, sections II–III](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2022-08/Multiple%20Dimensions%20of%20Private%20Information-%20Eviden.pdf);
[HRS public data access](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/about/introduction-to-hrs).
Public survey files require registration.
:::

## [Insurance]{.fg style="--col: #9a2515"}: findings

- No evidence that insured people are more likely to enter a nursing home
- Risk expectations predict both insurance ownership and care use, beyond insurers’ information

::: {.notes}
Both findings account for insurers' assessments of risk. The null result
for the standard coverage–use test coexists with evidence of private
information in the expectations data.

More cautious people also buy insurance and have lower subsequent risk,
which can offset selection based on expected need. The null finding helps
expose a limitation of the standard test and motivates a richer model of
selection.

Source: [Finkelstein and McGarry (2006), section III](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2022-08/Multiple%20Dimensions%20of%20Private%20Information-%20Eviden.pdf).
:::

## [Housing]{.fg style="--col: #107895"}: research question

How do large mixed-income housing developments affect municipal finances
and public services?

- Understanding local opposition to new housing

::: {.notes}
The paper is “Knock, knock: The impact of large subsidized housing
developments on the surrounding community.”

The question addresses a salient policy debate in urban areas: residents
may oppose development because they expect costs to existing residents.
New residents may increase demand for services, while new development
also adds tax revenue. The net effect is an empirical question.

The project began as Sethu Odayappan's Harvard undergraduate senior thesis.
Harvard's [thesis list](https://www.economics.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum5991/files/econ/files/archivedthesis1999_2023.pdf)
lists the title and David Cutler as the adviser. Use this as an example of
a question an undergraduate can pursue, without implying that a semester
project must cover every outcome in the published paper.
:::

## [Housing]{.fg style="--col: #107895"}: setting

- Massachusetts Chapter 40B allows zoning waivers for mixed-income housing
- Projects are built at different times with uncertain completion dates
- Difference-in-differences compares changes around openings across municipalities

::: {.notes}
Chapter 40B is the institutional context for the mixed-income developments.
Its comprehensive permit process allows qualifying developments to seek
waivers of local zoning. See [MassHousing's program overview](https://www.masshousing.com/en/programs-outreach/planning-programs/40b).
The repeated openings provide a way to study short-run responses.

Explain difference-in-differences verbally using one outcome, such as
municipal spending: compare the change in a municipality where a project
opens with the contemporaneous change in a comparable municipality without
an opening. The paper uses matched controls and a staggered event-study
design.

The causal interpretation requires parallel trends: absent the development,
the compared municipalities would have had similar changes. Uncertainty in
timing helps motivate the design but does not establish that assumption.
Pre-opening outcomes help assess it. Keep the distinction between project
decisions and actual openings clear.

Source: [published abstract](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1051137726000240).
:::

## [Housing]{.fg style="--col: #107895"}: data

Records collected and combined from state and federal agencies

- Treatment: Chapter 40B project decisions and opening dates
- Outcomes: population, public safety, schools, and municipal finances
- Sample: municipal panel covering years before and after project openings

::: {.notes}
Emphasize the range of records: familiar outcomes, less commonly used
municipal finance measures, and specialized records identifying the
housing developments. Combining them by municipality and year creates
the dataset needed for this question.

The published paper studies large developments built from 2002 to 2019.
The long panel allows the author to examine changes before and after
openings and assess whether pre-opening trends support the comparison.

The published abstract measures public safety using arrest rates. Do not
equate arrests with all crime. Likewise, a project's decision or approval
date is conceptually different from its opening date; the empirical design
must align outcomes with the relevant event.

The broad data-source description follows the instructor's account.
The [published article page](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1051137726000240)
says the assembled data are available on request. Public underlying
records should not be confused with a ready-to-download analysis dataset.
:::

## [Housing]{.fg style="--col: #107895"}: findings

- No detectable deterioration in municipal fiscal health or measured public services
- Population and short-run tax revenue increase

::: {.notes}
The null findings address concerns motivating local opposition. The paper
finds no detectable effects on long-run fiscal health or the measured
school, safety, and traffic outcomes. Increased tax revenue helps offset
the costs of additional residents.

These are findings about particular outcomes in this setting. They do not
establish that every effect of development is zero.

Source: [Odayappan (2026), published abstract](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1051137726000240).
:::

## Interpreting results

- A null result can challenge a nonzero prediction from theory or policy claims ([Abadie 2020](https://economics.mit.edu/sites/default/files/publications/StatisticalNonsignificanceinEmpiricalEconomics.pdf))
- A precise result can reduce uncertainty even when it confirms a prior, including zero

::: {.notes}
The first point concerns revising a prior. A simple adverse selection model
predicts a positive relationship between coverage and care use. Local
opposition to housing often predicts fiscal costs or worse public services.
The null findings are interesting because these contexts give us reasons
to expect a nonzero relationship or effect.

The second point concerns precision. A result can strengthen an existing
view by ruling out plausible alternatives, even if the initial expectation
was zero. Surprise is not required for a contribution.

In both cases, interpret the estimate and confidence interval. Failure to
reject zero alone does not establish a small effect or justify a large
revision of the prior.
:::
